inline.s: “Mahāmati, once the latent tendencies of all arising afflictions are cut off and the non-self of dharmas is realized — one sees that the flavor of samādhi is without real nature, and attains the unconditioned realm. Having attained it, one enters the supreme, supramundane unconditioned realm, perfects all the requisites, and will attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable, sovereign dharmakāya.”

Mahāmati, once they (the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) cut off the latent tendencies of all arising afflictions and wrongdoings, and eradicate the attachment to a self in dharmas, they are able to realize that samādhi too is an illusion, and no longer cling to its blissful flavor; thus they attain the realization of the unconditioned realm. Having attained it, they enter the Land of Eternal Stillness and Radiance (the supreme, supramundane unconditioned realm), fully perfect all the virtues, and will attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable, sovereign dharmakāya.

[Non-substantiality] Having no essential nature; an illusion. [Unconditioned realm] The sphere in which no afflictions arise. [Land of Eternal Stillness and Radiance] One of the four lands. Eternal refers to the dharmakāya, which is forever beyond arising and ceasing; stillness refers to liberation, in which all afflictions are forever stilled; radiance refers to prajñā, the wisdom that illuminates reality. These three virtues — dharmakāya, liberation, and prajñā — are the abode of all Buddhas, and so it is called the Land of Eternal Stillness and Radiance. [Four Lands] The land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together; the land of expedient remainder; the land of true reward and adornment; and the land of eternal stillness and radiance. The land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together is where common people dwell alongside the sages who manifest bodies and teach the Dharma in order to guide beings; the land of expedient remainder is where the two vehicles and those bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the dharmakāya dwell; the land of true reward and adornment is where the Buddha’s reward body and the bodhisattvas of the stages dwell; the land of eternal stillness and radiance is the land that appears as tranquility from the Buddha’s pure dharmakāya.

At that time the Bhagavān, wishing to restate this meaning in verse, declared: The vehicle of the gods and the vehicle of Brahmā, the vehicle of śrāvakas and of pratyekabuddhas, the vehicle of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas — these vehicles I have spoken. As long as the mind still turns, these vehicles are not ultimate; when that mind is utterly extinguished, there is no vehicle and no rider
no vehicle is established, and I declare it the One Vehicle
Only for the sake of guiding sentient beings do I teach the vehicles in their distinctions.
[Brahmā vehicle] That is, the bodhisattva vehicle. Brahmā means pure. The bodhisattvas, through the four immeasurable
minds of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, carry sentient beings across the sea of birth and
death; this is called the Brahmā vehicle. [Four immeasurable minds] The immeasurable mind of loving-kindness, the
immeasurable mind of compassion, the immeasurable mind of joy, and the immeasurable mind of equanimity. Giving
pleasure to all sentient beings is called the mind of loving-kindness; removing suffering from all sentient
beings is called the mind of compassion; rejoicing deeply when others do good or are
freed from suffering is called the mind of joy; and letting go of these three
without attachment, or treating enemy and kin alike without rising partiality, is called the mind
of equanimity. Because these four minds are universally directed to immeasurable sentient beings and give
rise to immeasurable merit, they are called the immeasurable minds. [The vehicles of gods, śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas] The vehicle of the gods is riding the teaching of the ten
wholesome deeds to be reborn in heaven; the vehicle of the śrāvakas is riding the
teaching of the four noble truths to realize the fruit of arhatship; the vehicle of
the pratyekabuddhas is riding the teaching of the twelve links of dependent origination to realize
the fruit of the pratyekabuddha; and the bodhisattva vehicle is riding the teaching of the
six perfections to realize the supreme, unsurpassed buddhahood. [No vehicle, no rider; no vehicle is
established] If the workings of the mind are utterly extinguished, then there is no one
who rides, and there is no vehicle ridden; moreover all vehicles are no longer established.

“The vehicle of the gods and of Brahmā, the vehicles of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the vehicles of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas — all these I have spoken. As long as the mind arises, these vehicles are not ultimate; when that mind has turned and ceased, there is no vehicle and no rider, no vehicle is established, and I declare it the One Vehicle. For the sake of gathering the foolish, I teach the distinctions among the vehicles.”
Liberation is threefold: the non-self of dharmas, liberation from afflictions and from clinging to wisdom
the attachment to a self in dharmas
“Liberation is threefold: separation from all afflictions, the non-self of dharmas, and liberation through the wisdom of equality.”

“For the sake of guiding the outsiders who grasp at a self, I speak of the tathāgatagarbha, that they may be free from the false views of an unreal self and enter the sphere of the three doors of liberation, in the hope of quickly attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

three gates of wisdom that lead into liberation: first, the door of emptiness, which realizes that all dharmas are fundamentally empty without clinging to emptiness; second, the door of wishlessness, which knows that all dharmas are illusorily existent and so has nothing to seek; third, the door of signlessness, which knows that all dharmas are without marks yet not without marks, and enters the middle way.
“Liberation is threefold: separation from all afflictions, the non-self of dharmas, and liberation through the wisdom of equality.”

This indicates that the three liberations spoken of here are: separation from all afflictions, the non-self of dharmas, and liberation through the wisdom of equality. This is likewise what the scripture’s passage and its context suggest, and so the annotation’s rendering follows it.

[Wisdom of equality] This is the wisdom of equality — the wisdom of the perfect equality of nature — one of the four wisdoms of the Tathāgata. [Four wisdoms] The Tathāgata’s four kinds of wisdom: the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of the equality of nature, and the wisdom of the great mirror. The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done is produced from the transformation of the five defiled sense-consciousnesses, and is the wisdom with which the Buddha accomplishes all beneficent deeds for sentient beings; the wisdom of wondrous observation is produced from the transformation of the sixth defiled consciousness, and is the wisdom with which the Buddha observes dharmas and the faculties of all sentient beings to prescribe the remedy suited to the illness and to turn the ordinary to the holy; the wisdom of the equality of nature is produced from the transformation of the seventh defiled consciousness, and is the wisdom with which the Buddha penetrates the principle of selflessness and equality and rouses unconditional great compassion toward all sentient beings; the wisdom of the great mirror is produced from the transformation of the eighth defiled consciousness, and is the wisdom with which the Buddha contemplates all phenomena and principles without anything left unclear — pure, luminous, seeing within and without, like a great mirror that illuminates all things.

It is like a floating log on the sea, ever turning with the waves; the śrāvakas in their folly are likewise, blown about by the wind of marks. Their arising afflictions are destroyed, yet the folly of residual tendencies remains; they delight in the bliss of samādhi and abide in the unconditioned realm, with no destination that is final

Yet they do not fall back; they acquire the bodies of samādhi and do not awaken for eons. It is like a drunken man who, when the wine wears off, then becomes aware; so too, when they awaken to the Dharma, they obtain the supreme body of the Buddha.
[Wind of marks] The two-vehicle practitioners have already left the mark
of a self in persons, but still cling to the mark
of a self in dharmas. The wind of marks here is
the wind of the marks of dharmas that causes them to
drift. The Diamond Sutra says: “Dwelling on no mark, thus does
one remain unmoved.” The practice of the One Vehicle is to
be unmoved by the wind of marks. [Mark of dharmas] Falsely
grasping that the method of practice really exists. [Method of practice]
The Dharma of cultivation — the means of ending birth and
death and realizing nirvāṇa. [Like a floating log on the sea,
ever turning with the waves; so are the foolish śrāvakas, blown
about by the wind of marks] This illustrates that the two
vehicles, not having cut off the obstruction to the known, still
take the marks of dharmas to be real, and so are
tossed about by the wind of marks, just as a
floating log is turned by the waves on the sea.

“It is like a log in the sea, ever turning with the waves; the mind of the śrāvaka is likewise, tossed about by the wind of marks. Though their arising afflictions are destroyed, they are still bound by residual tendencies, intoxicated by the wine of samādhi, dwelling in the unconditioned realm. This is not the final goal, yet they do not regress, for they have obtained the body of samādhi, and do not awaken for eons. It is like a drunken man who becomes aware when the wine wears off; so too the śrāvakas, who will become Buddhas after they awaken.”
Question: Many treatises speak of dharmas as having no self-nature, so why does the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra say
“as a cow has no horse-nature and a horse has no cow-nature, yet it is not that there is no self-nature”
Answer: The word self-nature has three meanings: first, the essential nature of a thing (its substance), namely the reality of all dharmas (see
); second, the innate spiritual faculty within sentient beings (see
); and third, the characteristic attributes of a thing.
[Attributes] The properties intrinsic to a thing itself — the necessary, fundamental, and inseparable characteristics of a thing.

Polysemous words in language satisfy the principle of linguistic economy — using a limited vocabulary to reflect the boundless objective world — but they also create a certain difficulty for our understanding. Therefore, when reading, one must always determine the meaning of a polysemous word in a given context.
The passage you ask about comes from the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:

“Mahāmati! As I have said that all dharmas are without self, because there is no self-nature within those dharmas I declare them selfless; yet it is not that dharmas are without their own nature — the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words should be known likewise. Mahāmati! Just as a cow has no horse-nature and a horse has no cow-nature, so dharmas are not without their own nature.”

Its meaning is: Mahāmati! As I have said that all dharmas are without a self, it is because there is no self-nature within dharmas that I declare them selfless (that is, dharmas are illusions), not that dharmas are without their respective attributes; the meaning of the words taught by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas should be known likewise. Mahāmati! Just as a cow lacks the attribute of a horse and a horse lacks the attribute of a cow, dharmas are not without their respective attributes.
In the passage above, the meaning of self-nature is the characteristic attributes of a thing.

In this passage, “all dharmas are without self” is spoken in terms of the reality of dharmas, meaning that dharmas are illusions. And “dharmas are not without self-nature (dharmas are not without their respective attributes)” is spoken in terms of the respective attributes of the myriad phenomena within the dream of ignorance. The central idea of this passage is: fundamentally, dharmas do not exist (“all dharmas are without self”); but within the world of forms in the dream of ignorance, they each have their own attributes (“dharmas are not without self-nature”). The former is spoken of the essence of dharmas, the latter of the marks of dharmas.

All dharmas are without self,” is also often expressed in the scriptures and treatises as “all dharmas are without self-nature (dharmas have no self-substance),” meaning that all dharmas have no real entity, are all illusions, like things in a dream. For example, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:

“For this reason, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of prajñā, if toward all dharmas he grasps existence, or non-existence, or both existence and non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence, or even non-grasping itself, then he is not practicing the perfection of prajñā. Why? Because
all dharmas are without self-nature and cannot be grasped.”
Here the meaning of self-nature is the essential nature
of a thing, namely the reality of all dharmas.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Ancestor says:
“When self-nature is deluded, that is the ordinary being; when self-nature is awakened, that is the Buddha.”
Here the meaning of self-nature is the innate spiritual faculty within sentient beings.
